# Arcade

> Arcade is the enterprise-ready actions runtime for AI agents.

Arcade is the enterprise-ready actions runtime for AI agents. We enforce your security policies on every action, execute reliably across any system, and govern agents centrally in production. Configure once and use any model, framework, and client — deploy the first agent the same way you deploy the hundredth.

Arcade delivers three capabilities. Enforce (Agent Authorization): deploy agents your security team approves — Arcade handles OAuth and manages user tokens, API keys, and secrets, then enforces your existing IdP, DLP, SIEM, and compliance policies plus per-action authorization at runtime. Execute (Agent-Optimized Tools): the largest catalog of agent-optimized tools — 7,500+ across 81 MCP servers, built for reliable execution at scale, not thin API wrappers. Govern (Agent Lifecycle Governance): a central control plane with a shared registry, version control, visibility filtering, and OpenTelemetry audit logs.

## Who this is for

Arcade docs serve two audiences. Start with the path that matches your goal:

- To build agents and tools (call tools, create MCP servers, ship user-facing agents), go to Build: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build. New to Arcade? Start with the agent quickstart: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/quickstarts/call-tool-agent.
- To deploy, secure, and govern Arcade for an organization (hosting, identity, gateways, audit logs), go to Operate: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate. New to operating Arcade? Start with the operator quickstart: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/quickstart.

## Getting Started

- [Arcade Docs](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/home): Arcade is an enterprise-ready actions runtime platform that enables AI agents to execute authorized tasks through optimized tools and managed lifecycle governance. This documentation provides guides, resources, and references for implementing agent authorization, integrating agent-optimized tools (MCP servers), and managing agent lifecycle governance.

## API Reference

- [Airtable](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/airtable): This documentation page explains how to set up and use Airtable authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access Airtable APIs on behalf of users through OAuth 2.0. It covers both using Arcade's default Airtable auth provider and configuring your own custom Airtable app credentials, including step-by-step instructions for creating an OAuth integration in the Airtable Developer Hub. The page is designed to help developers integrate Airtable functionality into their Arcade-based applications and agents.
- [API Reference](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/contextual-access-webhook-api): This page provides interactive documentation for the Contextual Access webhook contract, which defines the HTTP interface your server must implement to integrate with Arcade's system. It documents the default webhook endpoints (`/pre`, `/post`, `/access`, `/health`) and their request/response payloads, while allowing you to customize the actual paths in your Dashboard configuration.
- [Arcade API Reference](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/api): This page provides the complete API reference for Arcade, including the base URL, terms of service requirements, and an interactive Swagger UI interface for exploring all available API endpoints and their specifications. Users can browse and test the Arcade API directly through the embedded OpenAPI 3.0 documentation.
- [Arcade CLI cheat sheet](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/cli-cheat-sheet): This page provides a quick reference guide for all Arcade CLI commands, organized by category including getting started, authentication, contexts, organizations, and server creation. It's designed to be printed or used as a handy cheat sheet for developers working with the Arcade CLI tool.
- [Arcade MCP Server - Python overview](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python): The `arcade-mcp-server` Python package provides a FastAPI-like framework for building MCP servers, with the `MCPApp` class as the main entry point that handles tool collection, server configuration, and transport setup. This documentation explains how to initialize and configure the MCPApp, register tools and resources using decorators or imperative methods, and manage runtime APIs for tools, prompts, and resources.
- [Asana](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/asana): The Asana auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to call Asana APIs on behalf of users through Arcade, offering both a default Arcade-managed option and the ability to configure your own Asana app credentials. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating an Asana app, obtaining necessary credentials, and configuring the auth provider in the Arcade Dashboard for production use.
- [Atlassian](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/atlassian): The Atlassian auth provider enables tools and agents to authenticate with and call the Atlassian API on behalf of users, supporting integration with Jira, Confluence, and custom applications. This documentation explains how to configure Atlassian authentication in Arcade, either using Arcade's default provider or by setting up your own app credentials in the Arcade Dashboard. Users can then use Atlassian-powered tools and agents with proper authorization to access Jira and Confluence APIs.
- [Attio](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/attio): The Attio auth provider enables tools and agents to call Attio APIs on behalf of users, with options to use Arcade's default provider or configure your own app credentials for production environments. This documentation explains how to set up Attio authentication in Arcade, including creating an Attio OAuth app and configuring it through the Arcade Dashboard. Users can integrate Attio auth with the pre-built Arcade Attio MCP server, custom tools, or app code that needs to access Attio APIs.
- [Auth Providers](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers): This page provides an overview of authentication providers available in the Arcade ecosystem, which enable users to securely grant Arcade tools access to their data across various services like Google, GitHub, Asana, and many others. It explains that while Arcade offers built-in auth providers, users can configure their own to use custom branding, isolate rate limits, or integrate services without built-in support. The page includes a catalog of available auth providers with links to detailed configuration documentation for each service.
- [Calendly](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/calendly): The Calendly auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to authenticate with Calendly's API using OAuth 2.0, either through Arcade's default provider or by configuring your own app credentials. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Calendly developer account, registering an OAuth application, and integrating those credentials into Arcade for production use.
- [Changelog](https://releases.arcade.dev/preview/index.md): The Arcade changelog lists new features, improvements, and bug fixes across the Arcade platform, organized by release date.
- [Cisco Duo](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/cisco-duo): This documentation page explains how to configure Cisco Duo as an authentication provider in Arcade, enabling tools and agents to authorize API calls and access Duo-protected systems on behalf of users through OpenID Connect. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Duo OIDC application, configuring scopes and access policies, and retrieving the necessary credentials to set up the integration.
- [ClickUp](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/clickup): The ClickUp auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to securely access the ClickUp API on behalf of users through Arcade's authentication system. It covers using Arcade's default ClickUp auth provider, configuring your own ClickUp app credentials for production environments, and implementing ClickUp authentication in your application code or custom tools.
- [Context](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/context): The Context class is the primary interface that MCP tools use to interact with the server, client, and runtime environment, providing access to logging, progress reporting, resources, other tools, and language model sampling capabilities. Tools receive a populated Context instance automatically injected by the MCP server and should use its methods to communicate with clients and access runtime features rather than creating instances directly.
- [Discord](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/discord): This documentation page explains how to configure and use Discord authentication with Arcade Cloud, enabling tools and agents to access the Discord API on behalf of users. It covers creating a Discord app, setting up a custom Discord OAuth provider in the Arcade Dashboard, and implementing Discord auth in both app code and custom tools.
- [Dropbox](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/dropbox): This documentation page explains how to set up and use Dropbox authentication with Arcade Cloud, enabling tools and agents to access Dropbox APIs on behalf of users. It covers creating a Dropbox app, configuring the auth provider in the Arcade Dashboard, and integrating Dropbox auth into your application code or custom tools.
- [Errors](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/errors): This documentation page describes the exception types that can be raised by the MCP server, organized into a hierarchy of domain-specific errors for handling different failure scenarios like server operations, session management, request/response processing, and context management. It also lists convenience re-exports of tool-related exceptions from arcade-core that developers can import and use for error handling in their MCP implementations.
- [Figma](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/figma): The Figma auth provider enables tools and agents to authenticate with Figma APIs using OAuth 2.0, allowing them to perform actions like reading files, managing comments, and accessing team libraries on behalf of users. This documentation explains how to configure Figma authentication with Arcade, set up a Figma OAuth app, and integrate it with either the pre-built Figma MCP Server or custom tools that need Figma API access.
- [GitHub](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/github): This documentation page explains how to use GitHub authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to call GitHub APIs securely. It details why Arcade uses GitHub Apps instead of OAuth Apps, highlighting GitHub Apps' superior security features including fine-grained permissions, enterprise control, and compliance support. The page serves as a configuration guide for developers integrating GitHub authentication into their Arcade-based applications and custom tools.
- [Google](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/google): The Google auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to call Google and Google Workspace APIs on behalf of users through Arcade. It covers both using Arcade's default Google OAuth provider for quick setup and configuring your own Google OAuth provider for production, including supported scopes, limitations, and configuration options.
- [Hubspot](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/hubspot): This documentation page explains how to set up Hubspot authentication with Arcade, allowing tools and agents to access Hubspot APIs on behalf of users. It covers both using Arcade's default Hubspot auth provider and configuring your own Hubspot app credentials, including step-by-step instructions for creating a Hubspot public app and adding the necessary OAuth scopes.
- [Linear](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/linear): The Linear auth provider enables tools and agents to call Linear APIs on behalf of users, with documentation covering configuration options including using Arcade's default provider or setting up your own Linear OAuth app credentials. This page guides users through creating a Linear app, obtaining necessary credentials, and configuring the auth provider in Arcade's dashboard for production use.
- [LinkedIn](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/linkedin): This documentation page explains how to set up and use LinkedIn authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access the LinkedIn API on behalf of users. It covers configuring LinkedIn auth through the Arcade Dashboard, creating a LinkedIn app with proper credentials, and integrating LinkedIn authentication into your application code or custom tools.
- [Mailchimp](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/mailchimp): This documentation page explains how to set up and use Mailchimp OAuth 2.0 authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access Mailchimp Marketing APIs on behalf of users. It covers configuring Mailchimp auth using Arcade's default provider or your own app credentials, including step-by-step instructions for creating a Mailchimp OAuth application and registering it in the Arcade platform. The page is designed to help developers integrate Mailchimp functionality into their agents and AI applications.
- [Microsoft](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/microsoft): This documentation page explains how to configure Microsoft authentication with Arcade to enable tools and agents to access Microsoft Graph APIs on behalf of users. It covers creating a Microsoft app registration, selecting appropriate permissions and account types, and configuring the credentials in Arcade for both development and production environments. The page also lists the specific scopes required by various Arcade Microsoft MCP servers like Excel, OneDrive, and Outlook Calendar.
- [Microsoft Power BI](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/microsoft-powerbi): This documentation page explains how to set up and use Microsoft Power BI authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access Power BI REST APIs on behalf of users. It provides instructions for creating a Microsoft Entra app, configuring the necessary Power BI Service permissions, and integrating the auth provider with Arcade's Power BI MCP server and custom applications.
- [Middleware](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/middleware): This documentation page describes the middleware system in Arcade MCP Python, which allows you to intercept and modify MCP requests and responses through a chain of handlers. It covers the base `Middleware` class with typed handlers for different MCP methods, the `MiddlewareContext` dataclass that carries request information through the chain, and utility functions like `compose_middleware` for combining multiple middleware instances. The page also references built-in middleware implementations like `LoggingMiddleware` for common use cases such as logging and request tracking.
- [Miro](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/miro): The Miro auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to call Miro APIs using OAuth 2.0 authentication through Arcade. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Miro app, obtaining OAuth credentials, and configuring the Miro auth provider in Arcade's dashboard or configuration file. The documentation covers both using Arcade's default Miro auth and setting up custom credentials for production environments.
- [Notion](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/notion): The Notion auth provider documentation explains how to configure and use Notion API authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access Notion on behalf of users. It covers creating a Notion app, setting up the OAuth provider in the Arcade Dashboard, and implementing Notion authentication in both app code and custom tools.
- [OAuth 2.0](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/oauth2): This documentation page explains how to configure and use OAuth 2.0 authentication with Arcade to authorize tools and agents with any OAuth 2.0-compatible API. It covers supported OAuth flows (authorization code grant with or without PKCE), configuration steps for both Arcade Cloud Engine and self-hosted deployments, and how to integrate OAuth 2.0 into your app code and custom tools.
- [PagerDuty](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/pagerduty): The PagerDuty auth provider enables tools and agents to securely call PagerDuty APIs using OAuth 2.0 authentication on behalf of users. This documentation explains how to configure PagerDuty authentication in Arcade, including creating a PagerDuty app with scoped OAuth credentials and integrating it with your agent or custom tools. The page guides users through registering an app in PagerDuty, setting up OAuth scopes, and configuring the authentication provider in Arcade for production use.
- [Reddit](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/reddit): This documentation page explains how to configure and use Reddit authentication with Arcade Cloud, allowing tools and agents to access the Reddit API on behalf of users. It covers creating a Reddit app, setting up Reddit OAuth credentials in the Arcade dashboard, and implementing Reddit auth in both app code and custom tools. The page notes that Arcade includes a default Reddit auth provider for quick setup, but recommends configuring your own credentials in production to display your app name and manage rate limits independently.
- [References](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references): This page provides a comprehensive reference guide for Arcade's APIs, MCP servers, and client libraries, helping developers integrate Arcade's tool execution and authentication capabilities into their applications. It covers the REST API for orchestrating tools and workflows, the Arcade MCP framework for building custom MCP servers, and client libraries available in Python and JavaScript/TypeScript.
- [Resources](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/resources): This documentation page explains how to register and serve MCP resources in Python using the MCPApp framework, covering four registration methods: the `@resource` decorator for dynamic handlers, `add_resource` for imperative registration, and convenience methods `add_text_resource` and `add_file_resource` for static and file-backed resources respectively. Resources are exposed through URI-addressable endpoints and can include template parameters, metadata, and MIME type specifications to enable clients to access data over MCP connections.
- [Salesforce](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/salesforce): The Salesforce auth provider enables tools and agents to call Salesforce APIs on behalf of users, and this documentation explains how to configure it with Arcade by creating an External Client App, obtaining OAuth credentials, and retrieving your Salesforce Org Subdomain. The page covers setup steps for using Salesforce authentication with the Arcade MCP Server, custom tools, or direct API calls.
- [Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/server): The `MCPServer` class is a low-level API that implements the core MCP protocol server, handling message processing, middleware orchestration, and management of tools, resources, and prompts. It provides methods to start/stop the server, manage connections, and handle incoming MCP messages, with support for custom middleware, authentication, and context injection.
- [ServiceNow](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/servicenow): This documentation page explains how to configure ServiceNow authentication in Arcade to enable tools and agents to call ServiceNow APIs on behalf of users. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a ServiceNow OAuth application and registering it as a custom OAuth 2.0 provider in Arcade, with separate procedures for different ServiceNow versions (Zurich and later versus earlier releases).
- [Settings](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/python/settings): The Settings documentation describes the `MCPSettings` configuration container for the Arcade MCP Server, which uses Pydantic Settings to manage environment-driven configuration across multiple sub-settings like server identification, transport, middleware, notifications, and Arcade platform integration. It provides details on all available configuration fields, their types, defaults, and ranges, along with methods to load settings from environment variables and convert them to dictionaries.
- [Slack](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/slack): The Slack auth provider documentation explains how to configure Slack API access for tools and agents using Arcade, including steps to create a Slack app with appropriate scopes and add it to your Arcade project. It covers using Slack authentication in app code, custom tools, and the pre-built Arcade Slack MCP Server, with important notes about Slack's updated rate limits and API terms of service requirements.
- [Spotify](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/spotify): This documentation page explains how to configure and use Spotify authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access the Spotify API on behalf of users. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Spotify app, configuring custom OAuth credentials in the Arcade Dashboard, and implementing Spotify auth in your application code or custom tools.
- [Square](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/square): The Square auth provider enables tools and agents to authenticate with Square APIs using OAuth 2.0, allowing users to call Square services on behalf of their accounts. This documentation explains how to configure Square authentication in Arcade, either using Arcade's default provider or by setting up your own Square app credentials in the developer dashboard. It covers creating a Square application, obtaining OAuth credentials, and integrating them into Arcade for use in custom tools and agents.
- [Telemetry](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/mcp/telemetry): Arcade collects optional telemetry data from `arcade-mcp` users to understand feature usage, identify pain points, and improve the developer experience, while explicitly excluding sensitive information like tool names, parameters, and secrets. Users can easily opt-out by setting the `ARCADE_USAGE_TRACKING` environment variable either temporarily or permanently in their shell configuration.
- [The Arcade CLI](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/arcade-cli): The Arcade CLI is a command-line tool for managing Arcade deployments, generating and testing MCP servers, and handling authentication across multiple Arcade installations. This documentation covers installation and upgrade procedures for the CLI, as well as detailed usage of key commands like login, context management, and deployment operations.
- [TickTick](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/ticktick): This documentation page explains how to set up and use TickTick authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to access TickTick APIs on behalf of users through OAuth 2.0. It covers using Arcade's default TickTick auth provider, creating a TickTick app with proper OAuth credentials, and configuring custom TickTick authentication in Arcade for production environments.
- [Twitch](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/twitch): This documentation page explains how to configure and use Twitch authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to call the Twitch API on behalf of users. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Twitch app, configuring your own Twitch OAuth provider in the Arcade Dashboard, and implementing Twitch auth in both app code and custom tools.
- [X](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/x): This documentation page explains how to enable X (Twitter) API access in Arcade by configuring an X auth provider, allowing tools and agents to call X APIs on behalf of users. It covers using Arcade's default X auth provider, creating and configuring your own X app credentials, and implementing X authentication in your application code. The page guides users through setting up OAuth credentials in the Arcade Dashboard and provides code examples for integrating X auth into agents and AI apps.
- [Zendesk](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/zendesk): This documentation page explains how to set up and configure Zendesk authentication with Arcade, enabling tools and agents to call Zendesk APIs on behalf of users. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Zendesk app, obtaining OAuth credentials, and configuring the custom auth provider needed since Arcade doesn't offer a default Zendesk provider.
- [Zoho](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/zoho): The Zoho auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to authenticate with Zoho APIs using OAuth 2.0, either through Arcade's default provider or by configuring your own app credentials. It provides step-by-step instructions for creating a Zoho app in the API Console, obtaining client credentials, and configuring the necessary scopes and redirect URIs for integration with Zoho services like Books and Creator.
- [Zoom](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/references/auth-providers/zoom): The Zoom auth provider documentation explains how to enable tools and agents to call the Zoom API on behalf of users, offering both Arcade's default OAuth provider for quick setup and instructions for configuring your own Zoom OAuth app for production use. It details supported scopes, limitations of the default provider, and step-by-step guidance for creating and configuring a custom Zoom app in Arcade's dashboard.

## Documentation

- [About Arcade](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/about-arcade): Arcade is an enterprise-ready runtime platform that enables AI agents to securely take actions by handling authorization, executing tools reliably across business systems, and providing central governance. The documentation explains how Arcade solves three critical challenges: enforcing security through agent authorization and OAuth management, executing actions through 7,500+ agent-optimized tools, and governing agent lifecycles across organizations. It's designed for both agent developers who need to call tools and platform operators who deploy and govern Arcade for their organizations.
- [Add an MCP App to a tool](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/mcp-apps): This guide shows how to create an HTML user interface for MCP server tools and deploy them through Arcade, enabling interactive UIs like editors and result viewers within MCP clients. It covers attaching HTML resources to tools using the `@resource` decorator, deploying the server with Arcade CLI, and connecting through an MCP gateway so clients can render and interact with the UI.
- [Add metadata to your tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/add-tool-metadata): This documentation teaches you how to annotate MCP tools with ToolMetadata so that clients, policy engines, and tool-selection systems can understand what each tool does and how it behaves. You'll learn to classify tools by service domain, describe their behavior with operations and safety flags, and map those flags to MCP annotations that inform client decisions.
- [Add user authorization to your MCP tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/create-tool-auth): This documentation page teaches developers how to build MCP tools that require user authorization through OAuth, using Arcade's auth providers like Reddit to securely authenticate users before tool execution. It explains how auth providers work during execution, including the OAuth flow where users authorize actions and tokens are securely injected into the tool's context without exposing them to the LLM or client. The page provides step-by-step instructions for creating an MCP tool with authorization, including importing modules, setting up an MCP server, and defining tools with the `requires_auth` parameter.
- [Adding Resource Server Auth to Your MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/secure-your-server/secure-your-mcp-server): This documentation page guides developers on securing HTTP MCP servers using OAuth 2.1 Resource Server authentication, enabling tool-level authorization and secrets for self-hosted deployments. It explains what Resource Server auth is, why it's needed to protect HTTP MCP servers, and provides prerequisites and learning outcomes for implementing token validation and supporting multiple authorization servers. The page offers two configuration approaches for adding OAuth 2.1 compliant front-door authentication to validate Bearer tokens on every request.
- [Agentic development](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/setup/connect-arcade-docs): This documentation page explains how to integrate Arcade's documentation with AI coding assistants and IDEs by leveraging markdown-formatted docs and the llms.txt file format. It describes how AI agents automatically receive markdown versions of any docs page and how developers can configure tools like Claude Code and Cursor to access the documentation for improved code writing assistance.
- [Arcade Cloud infrastructure](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/arcade-cloud): Arcade Cloud is a fully-managed SaaS platform hosted in the United States that handles infrastructure, scaling, and operations while storing user data, monitoring data, and training data with various retention policies and encryption standards. The documentation explains data sovereignty, storage categories, egress IP addresses, VPC peering options, encryption methods, and provides users with control over data retention, deletion, and consent for AI model training through organization-level settings.
- [Arcade Deploy on your own cluster (Helm)](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm-arcade-deploy): This page guides platform operators on enabling Arcade Deploy in a self-hosted Helm-based Arcade installation, allowing developers to deploy custom MCP servers to their own Kubernetes cluster. It explains how deployments work (bundles stored in your artifact store, servers run as pods in a workers namespace), prerequisites needed, and how to configure bucket credentials for the Arcade Engine to access cloud storage.
- [Arcade Gateway Assistant](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/mcp-gateways/create-via-ai): The Arcade Gateway Assistant enables users to create and manage MCP gateways using natural language commands directly within their AI chat interface, without needing manual configuration. After setting up the assistant in an MCP-compatible client like Cursor or Claude Desktop, users can simply describe what integrations they need (like Gmail and Google Calendar), and the AI will automatically create a gateway with the appropriate tools from Arcade's catalog.
- [Arcade Glossary](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/resources/glossary): The Arcade Glossary defines key terms used in the Arcade platform, including agents (intelligent applications using LLMs), harnesses (the software that runs agents), tools (functions agents can call), and MCP servers (collections of tools deployed as remote processes). It explains important concepts like ReAct agents (LLMs that reason and act in loops), context (data passed to tools during execution), and distinguishes between protected/unprotected and project/global MCP servers.
- [Arcade with Agent Frameworks and MCP Clients](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks): Arcade integrates with popular agent frameworks and MCP clients to enable tool-calling capabilities in AI applications. These guides help developers authenticate with Arcade, load tools, and execute them within their chosen framework using code examples and configuration steps.
- [Arcade with Google ADK](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/google-adk/overview): This documentation page explains how to integrate Arcade tools with Google ADK agents, enabling them to access Gmail, GitHub, Slack, and thousands of other integrations. It provides setup instructions for both Python and TypeScript versions and outlines the capabilities agents can achieve, such as email management, messaging, and issue tracking.
- [Arcade with LangChain](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/langchain/overview): This documentation page explains how to integrate Arcade tools with LangChain agents, enabling AI agents to access Gmail, GitHub, Slack, and over 7,500 other integrations across Python and JavaScript. It provides setup guides for both languages and outlines the capabilities agents can achieve, such as email management, messaging, issue tracking, and web search.
- [Arcade with OpenAI Agents](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/openai-agents/overview): This documentation page explains how to integrate Arcade tools with OpenAI's Agents SDK to build AI agents that can access Gmail, GitHub, Slack, and 7,500+ other tools across both Python and JavaScript. It provides setup instructions for both languages and outlines the capabilities agents can achieve, such as email management, messaging, issue creation, and web search.
- [Arcade Worker](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/worker): The Arcade Worker hosts toolkits and executes tool calls for the Engine in self-hosted deployments, running as an MCP server with configurable settings for which toolkits to serve and pre-warm. It manages multiple toolkit versions in isolated runtimes, handles errors gracefully with retryable and non-retryable failures, and provides lifecycle management including runtime recovery, idle eviction, and graceful shutdown. Operators can control worker behavior through settings like `supervisor.prewarmToolkits` and `supervisor.serveToolkits` to optimize performance and resource usage.
- [Audit Logs for AI Agent Platforms](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/audit-logs): Arcade.dev automatically captures all administrative actions across the platform with details about who performed them, what changed, and when, accessible through a filterable dashboard and REST API. The documentation provides endpoints and query parameters to programmatically retrieve audit logs at the organization or project level for integration with SIEM systems, compliance tools, or internal reporting. It includes authentication requirements, rate limits, pagination details, and enums for filtering by action type and source.
- [Auth0](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources/auth0): This documentation guides users through integrating Auth0 as a User Source for MCP Gateways, allowing Auth0 users to sign in without creating new accounts. It provides step-by-step instructions for registering an application in Auth0, configuring callback URLs, and copying credentials to set up the integration in Arcade.
- [Authorize Existing Tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/langchain/auth-langchain-tools): This guide shows you how to use Arcade to authorize existing LangChain tools like Gmail without building Arcade-specific tools, handling token retrieval and management automatically. It walks through installing the arcadepy package, initializing the Arcade client, prompting users for authorization, and then using the obtained token to initialize and run tools with a LangChain agent.
- [Authorized Tool Calling](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/custom-apps/auth-tool-calling): Arcade's authorization system enables AI agents to securely access external services on behalf of users by handling OAuth 2.0, API keys, and user tokens. This guide walks developers through initializing the Arcade client, authorizing tools (like Gmail or Zoom), checking authorization status, and executing authorized tool calls, with Arcade automatically managing and remembering user authorization tokens for future use.
- [Build a Tool](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics): This documentation page introduces users to building custom tools using Arcade's MCP Server framework, covering the fundamentals needed to extend AI agents with new capabilities. It serves as a starting point for developers who want to create their first tool or add functionality to existing MCP servers.
- [Build an AI Agent and Workflow with Arcade and Mastra](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/mastra): This guide teaches you how to build a TypeScript AI agent using Mastra framework that integrates with Gmail and Slack through Arcade tools, enabling email reading, message sending, and automated workflows with built-in authentication. You'll learn to set up Mastra agents with tool calling capabilities, create multi-step workflows, handle authorization flows, and test everything using Mastra Studio. The guide covers key concepts like memory management, message processors, and tool configuration while providing step-by-step instructions from project setup through implementation.
- [Build an AI agent with Arcade and CopilotKit](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/copilotkit): This guide teaches you how to integrate Arcade's OAuth-backed tools with CopilotKit to build an AI agent that can perform actions like sending emails and searching news with secure user authorization. You'll learn to wrap Arcade tools for CopilotKit, render OAuth authorization as a generative UI component in the chat, and execute tool calls scoped to individual users without exposing credentials to the LLM.
- [Build an AI agent with Arcade and Spring AI](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/springai): This guide teaches you how to build a Spring Boot web application that integrates Arcade tools (Gmail and Slack) with Spring AI's ChatClient to create an AI agent that can call tools based on natural language prompts. You'll learn to configure the Arcade Spring Boot starter, expose tools using @Tool annotations, build a chat endpoint with tool calling, and handle Arcade's authorization flow.
- [Build an AI Chatbot with Arcade and TanStack AI](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/tanstack-ai): This guide teaches you how to build a browser-based AI chatbot using TanStack AI and Arcade tools that enables users to access Gmail and Slack through a conversational interface. You'll learn to integrate Arcade's tools with TanStack Start, handle streaming responses, manage authorization flows, and combine tools from different MCP servers to create a type-safe, provider-agnostic chatbot application.
- [Build an AI Chatbot with Arcade and Vercel AI SDK](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/vercelai): This guide teaches you how to build a browser-based chatbot using the Vercel AI SDK and Arcade tools, enabling users to interact with Gmail and Slack through a conversational interface. You'll learn to integrate Arcade's Gmail and Slack tools with Vercel AI SDK's streaming capabilities, handle tool calling, manage authorization flows, and combine tools from different Arcade servers in a Next.js application.
- [Build MCP Server QuickStart](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/quickstarts/mcp-server-quickstart): This quickstart guide teaches you how to build and deploy a custom MCP Server using the Arcade framework, starting with installing the arcade-mcp CLI and scaffolding a new server project. You'll learn to configure secrets, create sample tools (including one that requires authentication), and connect your server to an MCP client. The guide covers three example tools: a basic greeting tool, a tool that accesses environment secrets, and a GitHub integration tool that requires user authorization.
- [Build with Arcade](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build): This documentation provides guides for agent developers to integrate Arcade tools into their agents, build custom MCP servers, and deploy user-facing applications to production. It covers essential topics from getting started with tool calling to securing authentication and deploying applications on Arcade Cloud.
- [Build Your Own Contextual Access Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/build-your-own): This guide teaches you how to build a custom webhook server that implements Arcade's Contextual Access contract, defined by an OpenAPI 3.0 specification that you can use with standard code generators to scaffold your implementation. You'll learn which HTTP POST endpoints to implement (access, pre-execution, and post-execution hooks), what request/response fields each requires, and how to control tool access, validate/modify requests, and filter results.
- [Call a tool in your IDE/MCP Client](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/quickstarts/call-tool-client): This documentation page guides users through creating an MCP Gateway in Arcade to aggregate tools from multiple MCP servers and connect them to IDEs like Cursor or VS Code for use by AI agents. Users will learn how to set up an MCP Gateway with custom configuration, select specific tools for their workflow, and enable Tool Recommendation to optimize which tools the agent uses for each task.
- [Call tools from MCP clients](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/call-tools-mcp): This documentation page teaches users how to configure MCP clients to call tools from an MCP server using the `arcade configure` command, which automatically adds the server to the client's configuration file with support for different transport types like stdio and HTTP. It covers transport-specific configuration options, secret management, and customization parameters for popular clients including Cursor IDE, VS Code, and Claude Desktop.
- [Calling tools in your agent with Arcade](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/quickstarts/call-tool-agent): This documentation page teaches developers how to install and use the Arcade client to enable AI agents to call external tools like Gmail, Notion, and Slack. It provides step-by-step instructions for setting up the Arcade client in Python, TypeScript, or Java, and includes a complete example workflow that searches for news, creates a Google Doc, and emails the results to a user.
- [Capture mode](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/capture-mode): Capture mode records tool calls from AI models without evaluating them, allowing you to bootstrap test expectations and debug model behavior by seeing exactly what tools the model invokes. You can use the `--capture` flag with the `arcade evals` command to generate JSON files of captured tool calls, then review and convert them into formal test expectations for your evaluation suite.
- [Checking Tool Authorization Status](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/custom-apps/check-auth-status): This documentation page guides users on how to check whether tools have the necessary authorization and permissions before executing them, using the Arcade client in Python or JavaScript. It explains how to retrieve authorization status for all tools or specific tools, and defines the meaning of various status values like "active," "pending," and "completed" to help developers understand authorization requirements and availability.
- [Clerk](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources/clerk): This documentation page explains how to integrate Clerk as a user authentication source for MCP Gateways, allowing users who sign in through Clerk to access your Arcade instance. It provides step-by-step instructions for registering an OAuth application in Clerk and configuring the necessary credentials (Client ID, Client Secret, and Discovery URL) to connect with Arcade.
- [Comparative evaluations](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/comparative-evaluations): Comparative evaluations allow you to test how AI models select and use tools from different isolated tool registries (called "tracks") within a single evaluation suite, enabling side-by-side comparison of different tool implementations, providers, or designs. Each track maintains its own separate set of tools, letting you evaluate how models perform when given different tool options for the same task. This feature is useful for A/B testing tool implementations, comparing different tool providers, or evaluating alternative tool designs.
- [Compare MCP Server Types](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/compare-server-types): This page compares different MCP server types available in Arcade based on their transport method (stdio or http) and deployment location, showing which capabilities each supports such as handling secrets, authentication, and multi-user scenarios. The comparison table helps users choose the appropriate server type for their specific requirements regarding security, authentication needs, and deployment environment.
- [Configure Tool Recommendation](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/mcp-gateways/tool-recommendation/configure): This page guides platform operators on enabling or disabling Tool Recommendation for MCP Gateways through the dashboard or API, and explains how it works with the gateway's allowed tools to help agents manage large tool sets without loading all definitions into context. It covers prerequisites, step-by-step configuration instructions, and important details about default settings and API behavior.
- [Connect a Dynamics 365 Customer Service MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/dynamics-365-customer-service): This documentation guides users through connecting a Dynamics 365 Customer Service MCP Server to Arcade by configuring Microsoft Entra app registration and OAuth 2.0 settings. It explains how to provision the Agent 365 Tooling Gateway service principal, create a dedicated Entra app registration for Arcade, and set up the necessary permissions to enable access to Customer Service tools like case management and knowledge search. The guide covers both Microsoft-side setup and Arcade-side configuration while highlighting common setup mistakes and their solutions.
- [Connect a GitHub Remote MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/github): This documentation page guides users through connecting GitHub's remote MCP server to Arcade, which provides access to GitHub repositories, issues, pull requests, and other resources through approximately 80 tools. The page explains two authentication methods—fine-grained Personal Access Tokens or OAuth/GitHub Apps—and covers the GitHub settings and common setup mistakes users should be aware of when establishing this connection.
- [Connect a HubSpot Remote MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/hubspot): This guide helps you connect HubSpot's remote MCP server to Arcade by configuring OAuth 2.0 settings and setting up a HubSpot MCP Auth App, enabling access to CRM records, activities, conversations, and marketing tools. It explains key differences in HubSpot's MCP integration compared to other providers, such as automatic scope determination and Sensitive Data restrictions, and provides troubleshooting guidance for common setup errors.

You'll learn which Salesforce settings are critical for Arcade integration and how to diagnose common setup errors.

- [Connect a Splunk MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/splunk): This documentation page guides users through connecting a Splunk MCP Server to Arcade, explaining the prerequisites, authentication options (bearer token or OAuth 2.1), and critical Splunk configuration settings needed for the integration to work. It helps users understand which authentication method suits their setup and diagnoses common configuration mistakes that can cause silent failures during tool execution.
- [Connect an Atlassian Remote MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/atlassian): This guide explains how to connect Arcade to Atlassian's Rovo MCP server to access Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, and Compass tools, using Atlassian's OAuth 2.1 with automatic client registration. You'll learn to set up an agentic loop, add Arcade tools to it, and implement a multi-turn conversation system that handles tool authorization and execution.
- [Connect the AWS MCP Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers/aws): This guide explains how to connect Arcade to AWS's managed MCP Server using OAuth 2.1 authentication, where access is controlled entirely by the IAM permissions of the identity that authorizes the connection. It covers the setup steps on both the Arcade and AWS sides, including granting the necessary OAuth permissions to an IAM identity and understanding how the authorization model works.
- [Connect to MCP Clients](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients): This page explains how to connect various development tools and AI clients (like Cursor, Claude Desktop, and VS Code) to Arcade MCP Gateways, which enable agents to access and call tools from integrated services like GitHub, Slack, Gmail, and custom servers. The gateway acts as a control layer that determines which tools each client can access, drawing from Arcade's hosted integrations, remote MCP servers, or your own custom servers.

It serves as a central hub for getting help and connecting with the support team through various communication methods.
- [Contextual Access](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access): Contextual Access enables enterprises to control which tools users can access, validate tool requests before execution, and filter or transform tool outputs using custom logic hooks that integrate with Arcade's execution flow. The feature works through three hook points—Access, Pre-Execution, and Post-Execution—that let you enforce policies like role-based tool visibility, input validation, and output redaction without modifying your tools or agents.
- [Create an evaluation suite](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/create-evaluation-suite): This guide teaches you how to create evaluation suites to test whether AI models correctly use your tools by defining test cases that measure tool selection and parameter accuracy. It covers prerequisites, creating evaluation files, defining test cases with expected tool calls, running evaluations with different providers, and interpreting results using various critic types to validate tool parameters.
- [Create an MCP tool with secrets](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/create-tool-secrets): This guide teaches you how to build MCP tools that securely handle sensitive information like API keys and passwords by reading secrets from Context rather than directly from the environment. You'll learn to store secrets in multiple ways (`.env` files, Arcade Dashboard, CLI, or environment variables) and configure them so your tools can access them safely at runtime without failing due to missing credentials.

It also notes that if an MCP server already exists and is accessible over HTTP, developers should register it as a remote server instead of rebuilding its tools.

This guide teaches you how to deploy your MCP server using the `arcade deploy` CLI command, create MCP Gateways to select which tools to expose, and use Arcade clients to call those tools.

It emphasizes the importance of securely storing API keys since they grant administrative access to your Arcade account.

- [Group-Based Tool Access](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/group-access): This documentation page explains how to configure group-based access control in the Arcade Engine, allowing platform operators to restrict which tools different callers can see and use based on their identity provider group membership. It covers how enforcement works through tool matchers and access rules, and provides setup instructions for three identity backends: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, and SailPoint Identity Security Cloud. The feature runs natively within Arcade without requiring a separate server, making it ideal for multi-tenant gateway deployments.
- [Handle Errors](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/error-handling): This page teaches developers how to implement robust error handling in their tools using Arcade's error handling system to improve user experience and enable smart retry behavior. It serves as an overview that links to detailed guides on managing different types of errors gracefully in production environments.
- [Helm values reference](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm/values-reference): This documentation page provides a complete reference of all configurable values for the Arcade Helm chart version 1.11.2, explaining how to set them in a `values.yaml` file or via command-line flags during installation or upgrade. It details configuration options for Docker image pulls, registry credentials, and support images used by init containers, helping users customize their Helm deployment.
- [Hosting options overview](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy): This page helps platform operators choose how to deploy Arcade by comparing three main options: Arcade Cloud (fully managed), cloud marketplace deployments (turnkey solutions in your own cloud account), and self-hosted Helm deployments on your own Kubernetes cluster. It also explains related features like Arcade Deploy and Hybrid MCP servers, and notes that authentication can be customized even when using Arcade Cloud.
- [How Hooks Work](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/how-hooks-work): This documentation explains how Arcade invokes external webhooks at three key stages of tool execution (access control, pre-execution, and post-execution), and how to configure extensions and hook configurations to control their behavior, ordering, and failure handling. It covers the three hook points available, how to scope webhooks to organizations or projects, execution order rules, and what happens when webhooks fail or are unreachable.
- [Hybrid MCP servers](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/on-prem): Hybrid MCP servers allow you to run an MCP server on your own infrastructure (on-premises, private cloud, or VPC) while connecting it to Arcade Cloud, enabling secure access to private resources and sensitive data without moving them to the cloud. This guide teaches you how to set up a self-hosted MCP server with HTTP transport, create a secure tunnel to expose it publicly, register it in Arcade, and test it using the Arcade Playground.
- [Identity](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity): This documentation page explains how to configure user authentication for Arcade gateways and manage identity providers for your organization.
