- [In Custom Applications](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/custom-apps): This documentation section guides developers on integrating Arcade tools into custom applications by explaining how to handle user authentication, manage authorization, and programmatically retrieve tool definitions for building tool-calling interfaces. It provides the foundational knowledge needed to implement Arcade tools within self-built applications rather than using pre-built solutions.
- [Install the Arcade agent plugin](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-plugin): The Arcade agent plugin installation guide provides step-by-step instructions for installing Arcade across multiple supported coding clients and agents (Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, and others) to enable your agent to connect to apps through Arcade's hosted gateway using browser sign-in. The guide covers installation procedures for each client type, including special instructions for ChatGPT web users who must upload the plugin manually.
- [Internal networking](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm/internal-networking): This guide explains how to deploy the Helm-installed Arcade platform entirely within your internal network using an internal load balancer or Gateway API, with no public internet exposure. It covers configuration options for routing traffic internally, connecting to private MCP servers, and managing network access restrictions through allowlists.
- [IPv6 and dual-stack](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm/ipv6-dual-stack): This guide explains how to run the Helm-installed Arcade platform on a dual-stack Kubernetes cluster that supports both IPv4 and IPv6, and identifies which components still only support IPv4. It provides configuration values for binding addresses and IP family policies, verification steps, troubleshooting for common failures, and lists the specific features that don't yet support IPv6.
- [MCP Gateways](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/mcp-gateways): MCP Gateways allow you to connect multiple MCP servers to your agent, application, or IDE by federating their tools into a single endpoint for easier management and access. You can create gateways through a dashboard or AI assistant, control which tools are available, mix tools from different servers, and authenticate users through various methods including OIDC identity providers.
- [Microsoft Entra ID](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources/microsoft-entra-id): This documentation page guides users through configuring Microsoft Entra ID as an identity provider for MCP Gateways, allowing employees with Microsoft work or school accounts to sign in. It provides step-by-step instructions for registering an app in the Microsoft Entra admin center, including creating a client secret and granting necessary OIDC permissions, which are then used to create a User Source in Arcade.
- [Migrate from toolkits to MCP servers](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/migrate-toolkits): This guide helps you migrate your existing Arcade toolkit to the new MCP Server framework by updating dependencies, replacing imports, and creating an entrypoint file to run your MCP server. Key changes include renaming packages from `arcade-tdk` to `arcade-mcp-server`, updating the CLI from `arcade-ai` to `arcade-mcp`, and replacing `ToolContext` with `Context` throughout your code.
- [Okta](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources/okta): This documentation guides users through integrating Okta as an identity provider for MCP Gateways, allowing Okta users to sign in using their existing accounts. It provides step-by-step instructions for registering an OIDC application in the Okta admin console and collecting the necessary credentials (Issuer URL, Client ID, and Client Secret) to configure in Arcade.
- [Operate Arcade](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate): This documentation guide helps platform operators deploy, secure, and manage Arcade across their organization, covering deployment options, identity provider integration, and governance controls for tool access and auditing. It provides pathways for setting up Arcade Cloud or self-hosted instances, configuring user authentication, and implementing policies to govern how agents use tools.
- [Organize your MCP server and tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/organize-mcp-tools): This documentation page teaches you how to organize MCP servers and tools by defining them in separate files, importing tools from other packages, and combining them with decorator-based tools for better code maintainability. You'll learn the recommended project structure using a `tools` directory, how to import tools from both your own files and Arcade PyPI packages, and how to explicitly add imported tools to your MCP server application.
- [Platform architecture](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/architecture): This documentation page describes the architecture of a self-hosted Arcade deployment, including the services that run on Kubernetes clusters, how they interconnect, and their dependencies. It provides a reference topology diagram showing the complete deployment structure with network boundaries and data tiers, followed by a detailed table explaining each service's responsibilities and connections.
- [Private Registry](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/private-registry): The Private Registry is an authentication-gated portal where end users can browse the apps and tools available through an MCP gateway, see which tools require login, and submit or upvote requests for missing capabilities. Platform operators review all capability requests from their gateways in a centralized dashboard inbox and can respond to users, helping scale communication beyond pilot rollouts.
- [Providing useful tool errors](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/error-handling/useful-tool-errors): This documentation page teaches tool developers how to implement effective error handling in Arcade MCP by explaining Arcade's automatic error adaptation system, which converts common exceptions from libraries like httpx and requests into appropriate Arcade error types without requiring boilerplate code. It covers when to explicitly raise specific error types (RetryableToolError, ContextRequiredToolError, ToolExecutionError, UpstreamError) and how the framework categorizes errors like HTTP responses, network failures, and client construction bugs into structured error hierarchies.
- [Rate Limiting](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/rate-limiting): This documentation explains how to set up and use rate limiting in the Arcade Engine to control how frequently tools can be called, protecting upstream services from excessive usage without requiring a separate webhook server. Rate limits are defined as rules combining tool matchers, call limits, and time windows, and are enforced before each tool execution with counters scoped per tool and per organization/project but shared across all users. You can configure rate limits through the Arcade Dashboard or API, with options to set exact tool limits, toolkit-wide limits, or global limits across different time windows.
- [Remote MCP servers](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/remote-mcp-servers): This documentation page explains how to register and use remote MCP servers—servers hosted outside of Arcade by your team, a vendor, or a partner—within your Arcade projects. Once registered to a project or organization scope, a remote server's tools become available to all gateways, the Playground, and SDKs in that scope, just like Arcade's native servers, without needing per-gateway setup.
- [RetryableToolError in Arcade](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/error-handling/retry-tools): RetryableToolError allows you to retry a tool call with additional context by raising an exception that provides the model with improved information to refine its input parameters. This is useful when a tool call fails due to invalid inputs and you want to give the model clarifying details, like valid options, so it can make a better attempt on the next iteration.
- [Run evaluations](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/run-evaluations): The `arcade evals` command discovers and executes evaluation suites with support for multiple providers, models, and output formats. This documentation teaches users how to run evaluations with various options including filtering results, selecting specific AI providers and models, managing API keys, capturing tool calls, and exporting results in different formats. It also covers multi-run evaluation for measuring stability across repeated test cases.
- [Running a Server](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/contextual-access/examples): This page helps you quickly get started with Contextual Access by running open-source example webhook servers in Go, ranging from a full-featured advanced server with a dashboard to focused minimal examples demonstrating specific capabilities like user blocking, content filtering, and PII redaction. After running a server locally, you connect it to the Arcade Dashboard to create extensions and attach them to hook points for access control and content management.
- [Secure and Brand the Auth Flow in Production](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/user-facing-agents/secure-auth-production): This documentation explains how to secure authorization flows in Arcade.dev by implementing user verification to prevent phishing attacks, offering either the built-in Arcade user verifier for development or a custom user verifier for production applications. It provides step-by-step guidance on building a custom verifier route that confirms user identity before allowing tool authorization.
- [Securing Arcade MCP Deployments](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/secure-your-server): This documentation explains two methods to secure an unsecured Arcade MCP server: deploying it to the Arcade platform, which protects it behind Arcade's gateway with a randomized secret, or adding OAuth 2.1 Resource Server authentication to self-hosted deployments. The choice depends on whether you want Arcade to manage your server or prefer to host it yourself with existing OAuth infrastructure.
- [Security Research Program](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/resources/security-research-program): Arcade's Security Research Program invites security researchers to report vulnerabilities in their production services, APIs, authentication systems, and data handling through a responsible disclosure process via email to their security team. The program covers authentication bypasses, data exposure, injection vulnerabilities, and logic flaws, with researchers expected to allow reasonable time for fixes before public disclosure and to avoid automated scanning or unauthorized data access.
- [Self-host Arcade with Helm](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm): This documentation guides you through deploying the complete Arcade platform on your own Kubernetes cluster using Helm, covering prerequisites like Kubernetes 1.30+, PostgreSQL, Redis, and an OIDC identity provider. It walks you through setting up your identity provider, installing the Helm chart from the OCI registry, and configuring platform components, workers, networking, security, and telemetry through Helm values.
- [Server-Level vs Tool-Level Authorization](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/learn/server-level-vs-tool-level-auth): This documentation explains two complementary security layers in Arcade MCP servers: Resource Server auth that validates user access to your entire MCP server via Bearer tokens on every HTTP request, and Tool-Level Authorization that enables individual tools to access third-party APIs on behalf of authenticated users. The page provides a comparison table and guidance on when each layer is needed, with Resource Server auth being essential for production HTTP servers while Tool-Level Authorization is required for tools that access external user data.
- [Set up strong authentication](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/setup/strong-authentication): This documentation page guides Arcade Cloud users through setting up strong authentication methods—such as passkeys, authenticator apps, or security keys—to secure their accounts when their organization requires it. It explains why strong authentication is necessary, compares the three available methods, and provides step-by-step instructions for implementing each one in the Manage my account settings.
- [Setup Arcade with Google ADK (Python)](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/google-adk/setup-python): This documentation page guides you through integrating Arcade tools into a Google ADK agent using Python, covering project setup, API key configuration, and the necessary imports to build an AI agent that can execute tools following the ReAct pattern. You'll learn how to retrieve Arcade tools, transform them into Google ADK-compatible tools, and manage authorization while building an agentic workflow that can call tools to assist users with their requests.
- [Setup Arcade with Google ADK (TypeScript)](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/google-adk/setup-typescript): This guide teaches you how to build a TypeScript AI agent using Google ADK integrated with Arcade tools, which provides access to Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and thousands of other services. It covers the prerequisites, explains how Arcade's `toZod` function converts tool definitions to Google ADK's format, and provides step-by-step instructions for creating and running your first agent. The documentation also explains key concepts like authorization handling, session management, and how to extend the agent with additional tools.
- [Setup Arcade with LangChain](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/langchain/use-arcade-with-langchain-py): This guide teaches you how to integrate Arcade tools into LangChain agents by setting up the necessary packages, retrieving Arcade tools, and converting them into LangChain-compatible tools. You'll learn to build a ReAct agent that can use Arcade tools while managing authorization through LangChain's interrupt system and persistence features.
- [Setup Arcade with LangChain](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/langchain/use-arcade-with-langchain-ts): This documentation page teaches you how to integrate Arcade tools into LangChain agents by using LangChain primitives like agents, interrupts, and checkpointers to build AI agents with tool authorization support. You'll learn to retrieve Arcade tools, convert them to LangChain tools, construct a ReAct agent, and manage tool authorization through LangChain's interrupt mechanism.
- [Setup Arcade with OpenAI Agents (TypeScript)](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/openai-agents/setup-typescript): This documentation page guides developers through setting up an AI agent using the OpenAI Agents SDK for TypeScript/JavaScript with Arcade tools, enabling agents to interact with services like Gmail and Slack. It explains how to convert Arcade tools to OpenAI's format using the factory pattern, handle OAuth authorization automatically, and build a working agent with multi-turn conversation support.
- [Setup Arcade with OpenAI Agents SDK](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/openai-agents/setup-python): This guide teaches you how to integrate Arcade tools into OpenAI Agents applications by building a CLI agent that can execute Arcade tools with automatic authorization handling. You'll learn to retrieve Arcade tools, transform them for OpenAI Agents, build an agent using the ReAct pattern, and implement just-in-time authorization.
- [Stand up Arcade for your org](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/quickstart): This quickstart guide helps platform operators deploy Arcade, set up end-user identity management, create an MCP Gateway for agents and clients, and enable governance features like access control and audit logging. The page walks through choosing a hosting model (Cloud, marketplace, or self-hosted), creating administrator credentials, connecting an identity provider, configuring a gateway, and turning on security controls.
- [Stytch](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources/stytch): This documentation explains how to integrate Stytch as a user authentication source for MCP Gateways by configuring Stytch's Connected Apps feature as an OIDC identity provider. The guide walks through registering a Connected App in Stytch, obtaining credentials (Client ID and Client Secret), and configuring the necessary redirect URLs before creating the User Source in Arcade. This integration allows users who already authenticate through your Stytch project to sign in to your MCP Gateways.
- [The Arcade Registry](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/resources/registry-early-access): The Arcade Registry is a centralized platform where developers can share and distribute tools for AI agents, similar to HuggingFace or PyPI but designed specifically for LLM integrations. Unlike traditional tool libraries, it couples a runtime with the registry to collect real usage metrics and feedback, while also allowing developers to optionally monetize their tools. The platform supports multiple protocols through the Arcade Engine and is currently seeking beta testers to build and share MCP Servers.
- [Tool error handling](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/error-handling): This documentation page teaches users how to handle errors when calling tools from an Agent using Arcade's Tool Development Kit, covering structured error handling approaches, error types across different client libraries (Python, JavaScript, Java, and MCP), and best practices for robust error management. It explains Arcade's error hierarchy system, provides code examples for different programming languages, and directs users to debugging tools and resources for building error-resilient tools.
- [Tool executions](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/tool-executions): Arcade's Tool Executions page records every tool run in a project—including which tool ran, for which user, when, and its outcome—to help developers debug failures and operators review compliance and usage. The dashboard displays this execution history with filters for tool name, toolkit, outcome, time range, user ID, and errors, allowing users to drill into details like exact inputs and outputs (restricted to project admins). Developers can use this data to determine whether their agent sent wrong arguments or if the tool itself failed, while operators can track which tools are actually being used.
- [Tool Recommendation](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/mcp-gateways/tool-recommendation): Tool Recommendation enables agents to request only the tools needed for a specific task from an MCP Gateway instead of loading all available tools into context, reducing context window consumption and improving tool selection accuracy. When enabled, the gateway exposes two Arcade tools—`Arcade.SelectTools` to find matching tools by task description and `Arcade.UseTool` to execute them—allowing agents to dynamically discover and call tools in a two-step workflow. This feature is designed for gateway operators managing many tools and doesn't change authorization or policy enforcement mechanisms.
- [Tool Recommendation limitations](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/mcp-gateways/tool-recommendation/limitations): Tool Recommendation helps gateways with many tools by dynamically suggesting relevant ones to agents, but it's not suitable for all cases—it adds unnecessary overhead for gateways with fewer than ten tools, agents that already know their fixed tool set, or tools with poor descriptions. When using Tool Recommendation, plan for indexing delays on new tools, a limit of up to five recommended tools per task, and the fact that recommendations only cover tools explicitly allowed on the gateway.
- [Tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/resources/tools): Arcade provides a comprehensive ecosystem of AI tools that enable agents to take real-world actions, offering both a catalog of thousands of pre-built integrations for popular services and the ability to create custom tools using their development framework. The page guides users on how to explore existing tools, build their own, contribute to the community, and highlights key features like built-in authentication, production-ready status, and universal compatibility with any LLM or agent framework.
- [Types of Tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/improve/types-of-tools): Arcade offers two types of tools—Optimized and Unoptimized—that work seamlessly together but differ in design approach. Optimized tools are carefully designed to match AI chat interfaces and undergo evaluation to ensure reliability, while Unoptimized tools mirror original HTTP endpoints and require more careful evaluation before production use. Both types have identical interfaces and can be used interchangeably through the Arcade Dashboard or SDK.
- [Understanding `Context` and tools](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/runtime-data-access): The `Context` class provides tools with access to both runtime capabilities and tool-specific data, such as OAuth tokens, secrets, and user information, as well as features like logging, LLM sampling, user elicitation, and progress reporting. This guide explains how to use the `Context` object that is automatically passed to tools to securely access authentication credentials and leverage runtime features during tool execution.
- [Use Arcade in ChatGPT](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/chatgpt): This guide shows agent developers how to connect ChatGPT to an Arcade MCP Gateway by adding it as a custom MCP server through ChatGPT's plugins interface. After setting up an Arcade account and configuring an MCP Gateway with desired tools and authentication, users add the gateway URL to ChatGPT's custom MCP server settings and authenticate via OAuth. Once installed, users can then ask ChatGPT to execute tools from the connected gateway.
- [Use Arcade in Claude Code](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/claude-code): This guide shows you how to connect Claude Code to an Arcade MCP Gateway so that Claude can access tools you've configured in Arcade. You'll need an Arcade account and a pre-configured MCP Gateway, then add the gateway as a remote HTTP server in Claude Code using a simple command.
- [Use Arcade in Claude Desktop](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/claude-desktop): This documentation page guides users through connecting Claude Desktop to an Arcade MCP Gateway to access integrated tools and services. It provides step-by-step instructions for configuring the connection, including prerequisites like creating an Arcade account and API key, and setting up authentication through the Claude Desktop settings interface.
- [Use Arcade in Cursor](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/cursor): This guide explains how to connect Cursor to an Arcade MCP Gateway so that Cursor's agent can access and use tools like GitHub, Linear, Gmail, and Slack through a streamable HTTP connection. Users configure the connection in Cursor's MCP settings, then control which specific tools are available by managing the gateway's allowed tools list on the Arcade dashboard.
- [Use Arcade in GitHub Copilot](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/github-copilot): This documentation page guides users through connecting GitHub Copilot to an Arcade MCP Gateway, enabling AI-assisted development with access to custom tools across multiple IDEs including VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, Eclipse, and XCode. The page provides prerequisites such as creating an Arcade account and API key, then offers IDE-specific setup instructions with configuration examples and visual guides.
- [Use Arcade in Microsoft Copilot Studio](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/copilot-studio): This documentation page guides users through connecting Microsoft Copilot Studio to an Arcade MCP Gateway, enabling their agents to access external tools and services. The guide covers prerequisites like obtaining an Arcade API key and creating an MCP Gateway, then walks through the step-by-step process of adding the MCP tool connection with OAuth 2.0 authentication and authorizing access to Arcade resources.
- [Use Arcade in Visual Studio Code](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/mcp-clients/visual-studio-code): This guide walks you through connecting Visual Studio Code to an Arcade MCP Gateway so you can use Arcade tools within your IDE. You'll create an Arcade account, set up an MCP Gateway, configure it in VS Code through the MCP server setup, authenticate, and then start using Arcade tools in your agent chat.
- [Use Arcade tools with AG2](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/ag2/use-arcade-tools): This guide teaches you how to integrate Arcade tools into AG2 multi-agent applications by dynamically retrieving tools and registering them with conversable agents. You'll learn to build an interactive assistant that uses Arcade tools for Gmail and Slack while implementing secure "just in time" tool authorization.
- [Use Arcade tools with CrewAI](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-frameworks/crewai/use-arcade-tools): This guide teaches you how to integrate Arcade tools into CrewAI applications to build multi-agent systems that can interact with services like Gmail and Slack. You'll learn to retrieve Arcade tools, convert them to CrewAI format, create agents with these tools, and implement just-in-time authorization for secure tool access.
- [Use your own container registry](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/deploy/helm/container-registry): This guide explains how to configure a Helm-installed Arcade platform to pull container images from your own registry instead of Docker Hub, which is necessary for air-gapped environments, policy compliance, or avoiding rate limits. It covers setting up image repository paths, configuring pull credentials through Kubernetes secrets, and handling special cases like PostgreSQL, Redis, and Arcade Deploy runner images that have specific authentication or configuration requirements.
- [User Sources](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/identity/user-sources): A User Source connects an MCP Gateway to your OIDC identity provider, allowing end users to sign in with their existing identities instead of requiring Arcade to manage them separately. This documentation guides you through registering an OAuth client with your identity provider and creating a User Source in Arcade to enable production authentication for your gateways.
- [User-facing agents](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/user-facing-agents): This documentation guides agent developers on building agents that operate on behalf of end users with proper authorization and authentication. It covers production-ready security practices for user-facing agents, including secure auth flows, tool calling with user authorization, and integration with auth providers and identity systems.
- [What are tools?](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling): Tools enable language models to perform actions beyond text generation—like accessing documents, sending emails, or retrieving data—by calling external APIs and services. Arcade provides SDKs and pre-built integrations that make it easy for developers to securely connect LLMs with tools while handling authorization through standardized interfaces.
- [What's included](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/agent-plugin/whats-included): This documentation page describes the components included in the Arcade agent plugin, including an MCP server that provides access to over 1,000 optimized tools for connecting to external services like email, calendar, and chat applications. It outlines the available skills, subagent functionality, and provides a support matrix showing which features are available across different client platforms like Cursor IDE, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot.
- [Why evaluate tools?](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/evaluate-tools/why-evaluate): This page explains why evaluating AI tool-calling capabilities is essential before production deployment, focusing on validating that models select the correct tools and provide accurate parameters. It describes common failures that can occur without proper evaluation and details how Arcade's evaluation framework measures tool selection and parameter accuracy through scoring and status thresholds. The page also introduces advanced features like capture mode and comparative evaluations to help users test and optimize their tool implementations.
- [Windows environment setup](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/get-started/setup/windows-environment): This page guides Windows users through installing and validating the Arcade CLI tool using the `uv` package manager, with alternative `pip` installation instructions and troubleshooting steps for common setup issues. It covers prerequisites, multiple installation methods including optional binary package managers, validation procedures, and solutions for Windows-specific problems like execution policy restrictions.
